entities.name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Mosque of Ibn Tulun in Cairo, Egypt, built between 876-879 CE by Ahmad ibn Tulun (the Abbasid governor who made himself effectively independent ruler of Egypt), is the oldest surviving intact mosque in Cairo and one of the largest mosques in the world — a 6.5-hectare complex whose vast courtyard, unusual spiral minaret (modeled on the Samarra mosque in Iraq), and pointed arches (among the earliest in Islamic architecture) represent the high point of Abbasid architectural style outside Iraq. The mosque has survived virtually unchanged for 1,145 years.

Ahmad ibn Tulun, sent as Abbasid governor in 868 CE, quickly became de facto independent ruler of Egypt, using its enormous wealth (Egypt produced one-third of the caliphate's revenue) to build al-Qata'i — a new capital north of Fustat, centered on this mosque. The mosque's construction (876-879 CE) employed 300 Christian and Coptic craftsmen working under Muslim architects — an early example of cross-religious architectural collaboration. The stucco ornament style (carved stucco window grilles, decorative friezes) became definitive of Tulunid aesthetics.

The mosque's spiral minaret — a miniature version of Samarra's famous Malwiyya spiral — is unique in Egypt and directly references the Abbasid heartland. The pointed arches in the arcade (among the world's earliest surviving examples) may have influenced later Islamic and even Gothic architecture. The sabil (water house) added in 1296 CE by the Mamluk Sultan Lajin is a remarkable later addition. The mosque's survival through Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk, and Ottoman periods speaks to its revered status.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Mosque of Ibn Tulun — Cairo's oldest intact mosque, 1,145 years virtually unchanged — preserves in stone the moment when an Abbasid governor used Egypt's wealth to assert cultural independence, creating architectural forms (spiral minaret, pointed arches) that influenced Islamic and possibly Gothic building traditions.
